Function `render` is read only by the evidence of `requirements.cli.render`.
The requirement and its evidence file are deleted.
Deleted files have no coverage window, so `habeas status --coverage` warns about
`render` at once, before any further commit.
{test}`requirements.references.coverage.history`
rationale:
The example describes a concrete case with one expected outcome. `render` is read only by the evidence for `requirements.cli.render`. The requirement and that evidence file are then deleted. `render` gets a coverage warning at once, with no further commit. The test `tests/coverage.rs#fn[deleting_the_only_record_that_read_an_item_warns_at_once]` carries a {test} reference to this example.

**Setup.** `project()` builds a Git repo whose `src/lib.rs` has `parse`, `render` and `helper`. The test calls `record(...)` so that `rules.check` evidence reads `parse` and `helper`, and `rules.render` evidence reads only `render`. It commits, then asserts `warned(root).is_empty()`. That baseline shows every item is covered before the deletion, so any later warning comes from the deletion.

**Deletion and assertion.** The test rewrites `md/rules.md` so it defines only `check`. This deletes the `render` requirement. It also removes `evidence/rules.render.json` from disk, and it does not commit afterwards. It then asserts `assert_eq!(warned(root), ["render"])`.

**Why this covers the outcome.**
- The deleted evidence file's committed version still sits in Git history. If the implementation counted history for deleted files, `render` would stay covered and the assertion would fail. The assertion therefore checks that a deleted file has no coverage window, as `requirements.references.coverage.history` says (the window is the file's current contents on disk plus its past commits).
- The warning appears with no commit after the deletion, which matches "at once, before any further commit".
- `parse` and `helper` are not in the result. Their `rules.check` record still exists, so they stay covered. This shows the warning is limited to the item that lost its only reader.

**Minor point.** The test calls `habeas::coverage_warnings` rather than running `habeas status --coverage`. That function is the same source of warnings the status output uses. Other tests in the same file, such as `status_shows_coverage_warnings_and_says_when_history_is_incomplete`, check the status rendering. I did not treat this as a gap.

{impl}`requirements.configuration.feature_sections`
An item has recent coverage when it has a reference that covers it under
{cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_coverage`, or when its outline node, or
an outline node containing it, is named by file and selector in the inputs of
any version of an existing evidence record, citation review, or site review in
its coverage window. A file's coverage window MUST be its current contents on
disk, committed or not, together with its contents in each of the last N
commits in its Git history that changed it, read through a Git library rather
than by running `git`. A recorded hash MUST NOT matter here: an earlier version
names the node, whatever its code was then. N MUST be the workspace
`[coverage]` setting `reauthorings`, a positive integer, and 3 when it is not
set. When the history is unavailable, such as outside Git or in a shallow clone
missing those commits, the window MUST be the commits that are available, and
`habeas status --coverage` MUST say that coverage history is incomplete.
